name: Random Walk
description: You are given a tree consisting of $$$n$$$ vertices and $$$n - 1$$$ edges, and each vertex $$$v$$$ has a counter $$$c(v)$$$ assigned to it. Initially, there is a chip placed at vertex $$$s$$$ and all counters, except $$$c(s)$$$, are set to $$$0$$$; $$$c(s)$$$ is set to $$$1$$$. Your goal is to place the chip at vertex $$$t$$$. You can achieve it by a series of moves. Suppose right now the chip is placed at the vertex $$$v$$$. In one move, you do the following: choose one of neighbors $$$to$$$ of vertex $$$v$$$ uniformly at random ($$$to$$$ is neighbor of $$$v$$$ if and only if there is an edge $$$\{v, to\}$$$ in the tree); move the chip to vertex $$$to$$$ and increase $$$c(to)$$$ by $$$1$$$; You'll repeat the move above until you reach the vertex $$$t$$$. For each vertex $$$v$$$ calculate the expected value of $$$c(v)$$$ modulo $$$998\,244\,353$$$.
input_specification: The first line contains three integers $$$n$$$, $$$s$$$ and $$$t$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$; $$$1 \le s, t \le n$$$; $$$s \neq t$$$) — number of vertices in the tree and the starting and finishing vertices. Next $$$n - 1$$$ lines contain edges of the tree: one edge per line. The $$$i$$$-th line contains two integers $$$u_i$$$ and $$$v_i$$$ ($$$1 \le u_i, v_i \le n$$$; $$$u_i \neq v_i$$$), denoting the edge between the nodes $$$u_i$$$ and $$$v_i$$$. It's guaranteed that the given edges form a tree.
output_specification: Print $$$n$$$ numbers: expected values of $$$c(v)$$$ modulo $$$998\,244\,353$$$ for each $$$v$$$ from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$. Formally, let $$$M = 998\,244\,353$$$. It can be shown that the answer can be expressed as an irreducible fraction $$$\frac{p}{q}$$$, where $$$p$$$ and $$$q$$$ are integers and $$$q \not \equiv 0 \pmod{M}$$$. Output the integer equal to $$$p \cdot q^{-1} \bmod M$$$. In other words, output such an integer $$$x$$$ that $$$0 \le x \lt M$$$ and $$$x \cdot q \equiv p \pmod{M}$$$.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1823F — Random Walk [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
